{"content": "1|Discovery and Disaster
2|
3|    The courthouse on Centre Street at eight in the morning was a different organism than the one I'd visited to file my motion for Emma. During the day, it pulsed—a living system of lawyers and litigants and clerks and bailiffs all moving through the same revolving doors with the grim efficiency of blood cells through a vein. I joined the metal detector line behind a man in a camel hair coat who was arguing about merger law on his phone and a woman with a rolling briefcase who looked like she hadn't slept since the Clinton administration.
4|
5|    I was there for Noah Martinez's pre-trial conference, which was the court's way of saying *let's see if we can make a deal before we waste everyone's time with a trial.* I'd been dreading it for two days. Not because I didn't want a deal—a good deal could end this before Noah spent another night in a cell—but because I wasn't ready. I had questions without answers. I had a wall of color-coded folders and a list of suspects that included my own address.
6|
7|    ADA Ethan Moore was waiting in Conference Room 4C, which was less a room and more a repurposed storage closet with delusions of grandeur. He was younger than I'd expected—early thirties, with the clean-cut determination of someone who'd graduated near the top of his class and had been running uphill ever since. His suit was off-the-rack but well-maintained. His tie was silk. His handshake was firm in the way that lawyers' handshakes are firm: calibrated, deliberate, a negotiation before the negotiation.
8|
9|    "Ms. Walsh." He gestured to a chair that was slightly lower than his, which was either an ergonomic accident or a power move. In my experience, it was always a power motion. "Thank you for coming in."
10|
11|    "Wouldn't miss it," I said, sitting down and arranging my face into the expression Ira called my "litigator's poker face," which he said looked like someone had told me a joke in a language I didn't speak and I was too polite to walk away.
12|
13|    Moore opened a manila folder. One page. He slid it across the table. "Plea offer. Mr. Martinez pleads guilty to one count of attempted wire fraud, a Class A misdemeanor. No jail time. Three years' probation, full restitution paid in installments. He keeps his record relatively clean. He keeps his freedom."
14|
15|    I read the page. I read it again, because once was never enough and twice was the minimum for documents that could end someone's life as they knew it.
16|
17|    "No jail time," I repeated.
18|
19|    "None."
20|
21|    "For a case your office has spent six days building."
22|
23|    Moore's expression didn't change. "We've spent six days confirming what we already knew. The evidence is solid, Ms. Walsh. Signatures, bank records, cooperating witnesses. My offer reflects the reality that this office has limited resources and Mr. Martinez is a first-time offender with no prior record who we believe was a participant rather than the architect. We're being generous."
24|
25|    *Generous.* It was the word prosecutors used when they wanted you to feel grateful for the privilege of negotiating. I'd read about it in law school. I'd never heard it deployed in real time, in a repurposed storage closet, aimed at Noah Martinez—twenty-six years old, office manager, Friday donut guy, currently sitting in Rikers Island because someone had put his name on paperwork he claimed he'd never seen.
26|
27|    "I need forty-eight hours," I said.
28|
29|    Moore's eyebrows rose a fraction of an inch. "To do what?"
30|
31|    "To investigate. To review discovery. To advise my client based on something other than the assurance that you're being generous."
32|
33|    "Ms. Walsh." He leaned back. The chair creaked—his, not mine, which meant the ergonomic imbalance was a coincidence and not a psychological tactic, which somehow made it worse. "I'm going to level with you. This case isn't complicated. Your client signed authorization forms. The money moved. The account was in his name. I understand that new counsel sometimes sees complexity where there isn't any—it's natural, you want to do right by your client—but I'd encourage you not to make this harder than it is. For his sake."
34|
35|    The phrase landed in my chest like a stone dropped in still water. *Don't make this harder than it is.* Six words that contained an entire philosophy: the world is simple, the evidence speaks, stop asking questions.
36|
37|    "I'll take forty-eight hours," I said again, and kept my voice level, which took more effort than I wanted him to see.
38|
39|    Moore studied me for a moment. Then he slid the plea offer back into his folder and stood. "You have until Thursday morning. If you haven't accepted by then, the offer expires and we proceed to trial. And Ms. Walsh?" He paused at the door. "I mean it about not making this harder than it is."
40|
41|    He left. I sat in the repurposed storage closet alone for a long moment, staring at the chair he'd vacated, and thought about how easy it would be to take the deal. No jail time. Noah walks. Life continues. I could go back to my office above the laundromat and work on Emma's aroma nuisance case and Liam's poodle situation and the other small, survivable problems that had walked through my door before everything got complicated.
42|
43|    But Noah Martinez hadn't signed those forms. Or he had, and he didn't know why. Or he had, and someone had made him. And my address was on a filing for a fraudulent charity I'd never heard of, and M. Webb's signature was on invoices that moved two hundred thousand dollars, and none of it—none of it—was simple.
44|
45|    I gathered my papers and left.
46|
47|* * *
48|
49|    The hallway outside the conference rooms was a river of shoulder-padded suits and rolling briefcases, and I was navigating it with the focused aimlessness of someone who was looking for the clerk's office but wouldn't have admitted it if asked. I'd come to file a request for additional discovery materials—the system logs from Graham & Sundheim, the bank account opening records for the identity theft charge, everything Sophia had asked me to find.
50|
51|    The clerk's office was on the third floor, behind a set of double doors that were heavier than they needed to be, as if the building wanted to make a point about the seriousness of paperwork. Inside, a long counter stretched the length of the room, divided into stations by the organizational logic of someone who'd alphabetized their emotions. Behind the counter, three clerks moved with the particular indifference of people who'd processed ten thousand pieces of paper and had decided that ten thousand and one was not going to be the exciting one.
52|
53|    I was looking at the station assignments, trying to figure out which clerk handled discovery filings for criminal fraud cases, when a voice behind me said: "You're the Walsh lawyer, right? Cindy Walsh?"
54|
55|    I turned. A woman stood behind me—mid-forties, angular, with close-cropped silver hair and glasses that sat on the bridge of her nose at an angle suggesting they'd been adjusted one too many times and had given up trying to be straight. She wore a cardigan the color of oatmeal and a name tag that read HARPER DAVIS, COURT CLERK, with a small pin beneath it that I only later realized was a tiny enamel gavel.
56|
57|    "Cindy Lou Walsh," I corrected, because the "Lou" mattered and because I was tired of being called Cindy like I was someone's aunt. "Do I know you?"
58|
59|    "You don't. But I know your name from the filings. You filed a notice of appearance for Noah Martinez—that came through my station yesterday." She said it matter-of-factly, without judgment, which was more than I could say for anyone else who'd heard about my involvement in the case. "Harper Davis. I run the document review desk. If it's been filed in this building in the last six months, I've probably touched it."
60|
61|    "Then I need your help. I'm requesting discovery materials—"
62|
63|    "System logs, bank records, the whole packet. Yes, I saw your request come through electronically this morning. It's in the queue." She paused. Looked at me over the tilted glasses. "But Ms. Walsh, before you go further down that road, can I show you something?"
64|
65|    I hesitated. Ira would have said this was a trap—not a legal trap but a conversational one, the kind where a friendly stranger leads you into a cul-de-sack of small talk and you emerge twenty minutes later having revealed your entire case strategy and accepted an invitation to something you didn't want to attend. But Harper Davis had the specific, no-nonsense energy of a person who did not waste time, and I'd learned to trust that energy because it was the same energy I was trying to project and failing at.
66|
67|    "Sure," I said.
68|
69|    She led me to a workstation in the corner, where a computer screen displayed the New York Department of State's corporate filings database. She typed with the speed of someone who'd been typing the same website address for twenty years, which she probably had.
70|
71|    "The Noah Martinez case," she said. "Three shell companies are mentioned in the indictment. Evergreen Outreach, the Bennett Foundation, and Helping Hands Collective. You've seen the filings."
72|
73|    "I have."
74|
75|    "Look at the registered agent addresses."
76|
77|    She pulled up three separate filings, each one displaying in the blue-and-white format of the state database. Evergreen Outreach listed a registered agent address in Flushing, Queens—a residential building on 41st Avenue. The Bennett Foundation listed an address in Brooklyn, a commercial space on Atlantic Avenue. And Helping Hands Collective listed my address. East 7th Street. Above the laundromat. Suite 2B.
78|
79|    "Three different addresses," Harper said. "Three different registered agents. None of them are the same person. That's not unusual on its own—shell companies use mailing services, lawyers, whatever's available. But look at the pattern."
80|
81|    She pointed at the screen with a pen she'd produced from somewhere in the oatmeal cardigan. "Flushing address belongs to a retired postal worker named George Chen. I know George—he's lived in that building for thirty years. He has no affiliation with any of these entities. Brooklyn address is a co-working space that's been subletting to anyone with a credit card since 2019. And your address—" she looked at me, "—belongs to a lawyer who wasn't practicing a year ago."
82|
83|    "Someone's using new lawyers as mail drops," she said. "It happens. New attorneys print their addresses on business cards, on bar registration forms, on all kinds of public-facing documents. Their addresses are easy to find. If you're setting up shell companies and you need a registered agent address that looks legitimate but isn't traceable to you specifically, a solo practitioner who just hung out a shingle is perfect. Low profile, no compliance department, unlikely to check their mail for things they weren't expecting."
84|
85|    I stared at the screen. Three addresses. Three entities. Three people who didn't know their addresses were being used.
86|
87|    "This happens," I repeated. My voice sounded distant, like it was coming from the other side of the courthouse.
88|
89|    "More than you'd think. Especially with attorneys. Filings require a physical address, and new solos tend to use their office addresses for everything—it's right there on their bar registration, their letterhead, their website if they've built one. All someone has to do is pull the address from public records and plug it into the incorporation paperwork." Harper pulled off her glasses and cleaned them on the hem of her cardigan. "I see it every few months. Usually the lawyer doesn't find out until a server shows up with papers they don't understand. You found out through a case, which means you may have caught it earlier than most."
90|
91|    I should have felt relieved—relieved that there was an explanation, that I wasn't specifically targeted, that my address being on the filing was a crime of opportunity and not a deliberate choice. But the relief didn't come. Instead, something cold and methodical crystallized in my chest, because if someone was using random new attorneys as registered agent addresses, and those attorneys were innocently connected to the entities named in Noah's fraud case, then the person behind this wasn't just running a scheme—they were building a structure. A careful, distributed, deniable structure with other people's names and addresses as load-bearing walls.
92|
93|    "Harper," I said slowly. "If I gave you the other two addresses—Flushing and Brooklyn—could you look up who registered those entities? The incorporators, the organizers, anyone who signed the articles of organization?"
94|
95|    She put her glasses back on and looked at me. Something shifted in her expression—not surprise, exactly, but the particular alertness of someone who'd been doing a clerical job for years and had just been handed something that made the job interesting.
96|
97|    "I can look," she said. "Give me an hour."
98|
99|    I gave her the information. I waited on a bench in the hallway, watching the river of lawyers flow past, and I thought about my wall of color-coded folders. Green. Yellow. Red. Emma and Marcus Webb. Liam and the white van. Noah and the shell companies. My address on a fraudulent filing. Three separate cases that looked separate until you pulled back far enough, and then they started to look like the same shape seen from different angles.
100|
101|    In forty minutes, Harper Davis found me at the bench and handed me a printout with three names circled in red. She didn't say anything. She didn't need to.
102|
103|    I looked at the names. I looked at them again. Then I put the printout in my bag and walked out of the courthouse into the thin winter light, and I called Ira.
104|
105|* * *
106|
107|    Ira lived in a one-bedroom apartment in Washington Heights that smelled like instant ramen and isopropyl alcohol, which was approximately the combination you'd get if you asked a forensic chemist and a college student to cohabitate and neither of them ever cleaned. He worked nights at a private forensic lab in Midtown that I was never entirely sure he was supposed to tell me about, analyzing documents and signatures and security footage for law firms and insurance companies and the occasional private individual who needed to know if their business partner was lying.
108|
109|    He answered on the third ring, which for Ira at eleven at night was the equivalent of answering on the first ring for a normal person. "Cindy. It's late. Are you dead?"
110|
111|    "Not yet. I'm outside your building. I brought dumplings."
112|
113|    A pause. Then: "What kind?"
114|
115|    "Pork and chive from the place on Amsterdam. And I got the spicy ones you like."
116|
117|    The buzzer sounded before I finished the sentence.
118|
119|    Ira's apartment was exactly what you'd expect from a man who spent his nights examining the microscopic details of other people's documents: obsessively organized in some areas, catastrophically chaotic in others. His desk was a grid of labeled folders and magnifying lamps and reference samples. His kitchen counter was a graveyard of takeout containers in various stages of archaeological decomposition. The dumplings I'd brought joined a container of leftover pad thai from what appeared to be last Tuesday, on top of which Ira had placed a Post-it note that read, in his precise handwriting: NOT EVIDENCE.
120|
121|    He'd started doing that after I'd accidentally thrown away a sample he'd been analyzing—a water-stained envelope that turned out to be critical to a forgery case he was working on. The Post-it notes were his solution. Every leftover container, every piece of food, every object in his apartment that could theoretically be confused with a forensic sample now bore a small yellow square declaring its civilian status.
122|
123|    I set the dumplings on the only clear space on the counter—a six-inch radius around the soy sauce bottle that Ira maintained as a kind of neutral zone—and pulled out the authorization forms from Noah's file.
124|
125|    Ira washed his hands before touching them, which was both a professional habit and a personal compulsion. He put on nitrile gloves—he kept a box on the kitchen counter, next to the soy sauce—and sat down at his desk under the magnifying lamp like a surgeon preparing for an operation.
126|
127|    "Walk me through it," he said, adjusting the lamp.
128|

function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

cross_profile.description: Opt out of the cross-profile soft guard. Defaults to false. Set true ONLY after explicit user direction to edit another Hermes profile's skills/plugins/cron/memories.

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — bg without notify runs SILENTLY and you have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself. Two legitimate uses:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — silent is correct, there's no exit to notify on.
  (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — MUST set notify_on_complete=true. Without it you'll either forget to poll or sit blocked waiting for the user to surface the result.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — without it, the process runs silently and you'll have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself (easy to forget, leading to silent blindness on long jobs). Two legitimate patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — these stay silent because there's no exit to notify on. (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — these MUST set notify_on_complete=true. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.
